en: The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata, in one fascicle,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery, by Imperial Decree.
At one time, the Buddha was at Vaiśālī beneath the Tree of Melodious Sound,
together with thirty-six thousand great bodhisattvas, eighty thousand bhikṣus,
the twelve divine kings along with their retinues, and the great divine kings of the eight classes of beings— devas, nāgas, and so forth.
Having thus spoken this Dharma within such a great assembly,
there was no one among the multitude who did not rejoice upon hearing it.
This is called the *pranidhāna-mantra* (vow-mantra). The Bhagavat then spoke the mantra, saying:
*Namo bhagavate vīrasena-vīrabhadra-vaiḍūryaprabharājāya tathāgatāya | tadyathā | oṃ vīrasme vīrasme vīrasena-samudgate svāhā.* If there be anyone who receives and maintains this *dhāraṇī*:
It can uproot all grave offenses from past births and deaths within one's own body;
one shall no longer undergo the three miserable realms,
escape the nine untimely deaths, and transcend all sufferings.
In every place throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is peace and happiness;
such is the spontaneous and unimpeded nature of the Dharma.
If there are sons or daughters of good family, etc., [who practice accordingly...]
Those who uphold, recite, and chant this mantra should diligently practice day and night, bathing with fragrant water and wearing fresh, clean garments,
while observing all the prohibitive precepts according to the Dharma.
Having completed one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra,
go to a pure location and prepare the ground according to the Dharma;
construct it with clean earth and level it.
Mix pure cow dung with sandalwood to smear upon a circular maṇḍala.
Adorn the maṇḍala with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels.
Place an image of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru at the center, with the Tathāgata’s left hand holding a medicinal vessel.
It is also called the Priceless Jewel.
With his right hand, he forms the Seal of Binding the Three Realms.
Having donned the kāṣāya, he sits in the full lotus posture.
He caused them to be placed upon a lotus pedestal;
beneath the pedestal were twelve divine generals,
with eighty-four thousand retinues as their leaders.
Furthermore, one should provide a lotus pedestal.
Within the majestic radiance of the Tathāgata, one should place the two bodhisattvas, Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha.
Thus, the four sides of the maṇḍala are encircled by five colors.
Approaching the image, place two *argha* vessels— one of conch shell and one of clay—
and perform the service of offering and worship according to your preference.
Recite the mantra before the image for a period of forty-nine days.
If, for twenty-one days,
one places auspicious vases at the four corners of the image altar;
thus, within seven days and nights—
If one recites the mantra a full hundred thousand times, ten million times,
or more, whatever one seeks will be fulfilled according to one's heart, and immeasurable fruits and rewards will be obtained—
except in cases where one lacks a sincere mind.
The Dharma should be thus.
All its benefits cannot be fully described;
its remaining powers cannot be told even at the end of an eon.
Furthermore, the fundamental mudrā of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata is described as follows:
with the left and right hands, interlace the eight fingers from the index fingers downward,
turning them inward so they enter the palms.
Move the two thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is:
Oṃ canda-kīli svāhā. This is called the Root Mudrā. Next, the Arghya Mudrā is explained.
Hold the vessel with both palms and carry it upon the crown of the head.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ karkarūṃ sama-sama svāhā*. Next is the flower-seat mantra and mudrā. Next, the incense-smearing mudrā is explained: join the two palms; bring the tips of the two index fingers and the two thumbs together as if snapping the fingers.
The mantra is: Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ kṣantukārāya svāhā. Next, the Flower Mudrā is explained: join the two hands in *añjali* and slightly open the tips of the two little fingers.
The mantra is: Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mucye svāhā. Next, the incense mudrā is explained: join the two hands in *añjali* and bend the middle fingers like a mountain.

The mantra is: Oṃ namo kṣarakṣaramaṇḍalavisaye śānti svāhā. Next, the Flower Seat Mudrā is explained: join the backs of both hands together and press the right wrist against the left. The mantra is: [as above].
Oṃ sarva-saṃskāra-maṭha. Next, he taught the seal of universal offering (*sarvapūjāmudrā*): join the two hands in the vajra-pañjali gesture.
The mantra is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ avahana-maṇi svāhā.* Next, perform the recitation. Then, perform the dismissal: take a flower with the *dhyāna* and *jñāna* fingers and cast it into the center of the maṇḍala.
The mantra is: Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, agne coge coge svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra is able to extinguish all suffering and affliction.
If there are persons who have many karmic obstacles, as well as women.
Wishing to turn away misfortune,
they followed the instructions to fashion a single image of Bhaisajyaguru and transcribe one scroll of the Bhaisajyaguru Sutra.
Construct forty-nine banners and forty-nine lamps, arranging them in seven tiers in the shape of a chariot wheel,
and place them before the image.
Make a cord using five colors.
Seal it with the mudrā.
Tie forty-nine knots around that person’s body.
Furthermore, recite the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* forty-nine times.
All karmic obstacles and hindrances shall be liberated.
One’s lifespan will be extended, one shall not encounter untimely suffering, and one will attain peace and stability.
As for diseases caused by ghosts and spirits...
The affliction will be immediately cured.
If one wishes to subdue wicked people,
one should form the mudrā and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with a mind of wrath.
It strikes down all externalists from afar, utterly destroying them.
If anyone suffers from a heart disease,
by consecrating *agaru* (sandalwood) and applying it to the heart, they will be healed.
If a person suffers from a headache,
empower cinnamon twenty times;
by consuming it, they will be cured.
If a person suffers from swelling or jaundice, they should empower saffron one hundred and eight times and apply it; the affliction will be eliminated and cured.
If a person wishes to distance themselves from an enemy, [they should do so].
Consecrate one hundred and eight *kuliñja* seeds with mantras;
recite the mantra once for each seed as you burn them, casting them into the fire.
That person will immediately depart to a distance.
If one suffers from pain in the limbs and joints,
one should recite the mantra over boiling water one hundred and eight times;
by bathing with it, the ailment will be immediately cured.
If a person, every morning at dawn,
takes a handful of water and drinks it after reciting the mantra seven times,
all evil retributions within their body will be completely extinguished.
How much more so for those who are free from all calamities;
their sufferings of the three karmas shall likewise be healed and cured,
and they shall obtain a long life.
If one drinks or eats [food] while reciting this mantra,
no poisons whatsoever shall be able to cause harm.
If one encounters wicked people or enemies...
One should recite this mantra.
All enemies who give rise to malicious intent shall be subdued;
their evil minds will immediately be extinguished, and they will turn toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
In places where there is fear,
one must collect the mind and perform recitation.
When wishing to lie down, [one should likewise do so].
When one recites this mantra one hundred and eight times,
one will immediately obtain auspicious dreams and clearly discern good and bad fortune.
If a person suffers from malaria, [they shall be cured].
One who upholds this mantra should look upon the person afflicted with malaria and recite it one thousand and eight times with earnest diligence;
their affliction will then be immediately eliminated and healed.

*The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Medicine Master Tathāgata*, one fascicle. Completed copying on the second day of the second month in the third year of the Hōgen era at the hour of the Rooster (18:00–20:00). Respectfully transcribed from the original manuscript of the Daidenbō Hōin. Presented as a gift to future worthies, hoping that we may together aspire toward the Buddha-wisdom. Written by the Dharma-seeking śramaṇa Kakujō on the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Enpō era (1674), the Year of the Tiger, using a copy from the Hōkudō platform of Kōzan-ji; proofread once. By Noyazawa Matsuji Shōgon, age thirty-six. Copied on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Tenmei era (1781), the Year of the Ox, using the manuscript of the monk Kakuen. By Jinin. Recorded in the first year of the Kyowa era (1801), the Year of the Dog.
I have sought the original text and its national-character (Chinese) glosses for the aforementioned *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra Recitation Ritual*.
Since the woodblocks were carved during the Gen’i era, [the text has been widely circulated].
However, the original manuscript from which this was copied lacked one sheet; therefore,
it has been further collated and carved upon wooden printing blocks to ensure its longevity.

Recorded by the śramaṇa Kaidō while residing at Chōgaku on Mount Hōzan; completed with revisions and annotations on the tenth day of the fourth month of the Ki-hai year of the Kyōwa era (1813) by Jishun.
